title: まい: the negative helper
summary: まい is the negative volitional: it says something is unlikely, or that you firmly will not do it.

blocks.text: **まい** is an old-fashioned negative helper, a cousin of ない. It is a negative **volitional**: where ~よう means "will / let's", ~まい means "will not / surely not". It never changes (no past, no て-form), and it has two common jobs, plus two set patterns.
まい is usually stuck on the end of the dictionary form: 行くまい, 食べるまい. An ichidan verb can also lose its る (見まい), and the two irregulars have extra forms: する → するまい / しまい, 来る → 来るまい / こまい.
This is the most common use. It is the negative partner of でしょう / だろう, and it can attach straight to a verb, which the positive volitional cannot.

blocks.en: There is surely no such story.

blocks.jp: この雨では、彼は来るまい。
blocks.en: In this rain, he will surely not come.

blocks.text: あるまい means the same as ないだろう, and ではあるまい means ではないだろう.
A firm resolution not to do something.

blocks.jp: 買おうか買うまいか迷う。
blocks.en: I can't decide whether to buy it or not.

blocks.jp: 子供ではあるまいし、泣くな。
blocks.en: You are not a child, so don't cry.

blocks.text: The positive and negative volitional together mean "whether or not". Adding し to まい gives "it's not as if ...".

items: まい = negative volitional: **unlikely** or **I will never**.
It does not make a negative invitation: 行くまい does not mean "let's not go".
Set patterns: ～ようか～まいか (whether or not), ～まいし (it's not as if).
